opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think inference is actually where architectures like Mamba really shine. If you look at how people use models now, a lot of the cost has shifted from training to inference. You've got long contexts, agents running many steps, reasoning models generating thousands of tokens before they answer. All of that is inference-heavy.

With a Transformer, the fundamental bottleneck during generation is the KV cache. Every new token has to attend to every previous token, so memory grows linearly with context length, and you're constantly moving that cache in and out of GPU memory. Decoding ends up memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. That limits your batch size and your throughput, especially for long sequences.

State space models like Mamba take a different approach. You compress the history into a fixed-size state, so the cost of generating each new token is constant regardless of how long the context is. No growing KV cache. In practice that means you can fit much larger batches and get several times higher throughput, and the advantage grows as sequences get longer.

Of course there's a trade-off. Compressing everything into a fixed state means you lose some ability to do precise recall, like copying exact information from far back in the context. Attention is very good at that. So what we've seen work really well, and what a lot of groups have converged on, is hybrid models: mostly Mamba or linear-attention-style layers, with a few attention layers mixed in. You get most of the quality of a Transformer and most of the inference efficiency of an SSM.

I think going forward, architecture and hardware-aware design will be one of the biggest levers for inference cost. It's not just about the math of the layer. It's about whether that layer maps well onto the hardware, whether it uses tensor cores, how it handles memory. That's been a theme in my work since FlashAttention. And as workloads keep shifting toward long-context and test-time compute, I expect these more efficient architectures, especially hybrids, to become a bigger and bigger part of what gets deployed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that inference is increasingly becoming the dominant cost, right? Training, you do it once, but inference you're doing it over and over, and with things like chain-of-thought and agents, the amount of tokens you're generating per query is just going up. So the question is, what's the bottleneck at inference time? And for Transformers, when you're doing autoregressive decoding, the bottleneck is really the KV cache. Every token you generate, you have to read the entire KV cache from memory, and that cache grows linearly with sequence length. So for long contexts, you're memory-bandwidth bound, and that's what limits your throughput and your latency.

What Mamba and state space models more generally do is they compress that whole history into a fixed-size state. So instead of a cache that grows with the sequence, you have this constant-size state, and generating the next token is just a constant amount of memory traffic regardless of how long the context is. That means decoding is much faster, especially for long sequences, and you can fit a lot more sequences into a batch because you're not spending all your GPU memory on cache. So you get higher throughput as well.

Now, I don't think it's going to be "SSMs replace attention entirely." Attention is really good at precise retrieval, copying from the context, that kind of thing, and the fixed state in Mamba does have limits on how much it can remember exactly. So what we're seeing, and what I think makes the most sense, is hybrid architectures. You keep a small number of attention layers for that retrieval capability, and most of the layers are Mamba layers. You still get most of the inference speedup, because the KV cache is now maybe a tenth of the size or smaller, but you keep the quality.

The other thing I'd say is that the architecture and the hardware really have to be co-designed. Mamba-2 was partly about reformulating the state space model so that the core computation looks like matrix multiplications, which means it can run on tensor cores, which is where all the FLOPs on modern GPUs are. So part of the gains in inference speed come from the algorithmic side, the smaller state, and part come from just making sure the operations map well onto the hardware. I think there's a lot more to do there, including things like how you do speculative decoding with these models, how you quantize the state, and so on. But overall I'm pretty optimistic that for inference-heavy workloads, these kinds of architectures are going to give us maybe several-x improvements in throughput, and that compounds with all the systems work people are doing.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to rethink how much information we need to carry forward during generation. With a Transformer, you keep a KV cache that grows with the sequence, and each new token requires reading that history. As context gets longer, moving that data becomes a substantial part of the cost.

With Mamba, you carry forward a fixed-size state and update it as new tokens arrive. That makes the memory requirements much more predictable and can make decoding faster, especially at long contexts or when you want to serve larger batches.

The tradeoff is that you’re compressing the history into that state. Attention is useful when you need to look back and retrieve something very specific. So I’m excited about hybrid architectures that use state-space layers for much of the processing and attention where it adds the most value.

Ultimately, the comparison has to be at comparable model quality. You need the architecture, the training recipe, and the hardware implementation to work together to turn that efficiency potential into actual inference gains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main opportunity is to rethink how much information we need to move around during inference. With a Transformer, as you generate more tokens, you keep a growing KV cache, and you have to read that cache to produce each new token. That can become expensive, especially for long contexts.

With an architecture like Mamba, you compress the history into a fixed-size state that you update as new tokens arrive. So the memory requirements don’t grow with the sequence length in the same way. That creates an opportunity for faster generation and larger batch sizes.

But the architecture and the implementation have to go together. You need to organize those state updates so they run efficiently on the hardware, and you need to maintain model quality. I think hybrid architectures are also interesting: use attention where access to specific tokens is valuable, and use state-space layers where a compact state is sufficient. The question is which combination gives you the best quality at a given inference cost.
